rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.3-2.5 and 3.2-3.3 report the authors' own two-season field monitoring (2018-2019) with Sentek capacitance probes in 4-5 commercial potato fields at NAPI, New Mexico, plus water-balance, FAO-56 and OpenET ET estimates.
rows.notes: The study reports no tuber yield data at all, no control (non-sensor) plots, and no comparison of yields between sensor-scheduled and conventionally scheduled fields. The 6.6% yield increase, 15% water reduction and farmer-reported time savings in the passage do not appear anywhere in this paper. What the study actually shows is soil water dynamics by depth (most variation in 0-40 cm, little in 40-60 cm), an effective rooting zone of about 40 cm, seasonal applied irrigation of 777 <U+00B1> 36 mm, and seasonal ET of 580 <U+00B1> 38 mm (2018) and 645 <U+00B1> 57 mm (2019) by soil water balance versus higher FAO two-step and OpenET values. Sensor-based soil water monitoring is at most a precondition for the claimed yield benefit, so upstream is set to true.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.3-2.5 and 3.2-3.3 report the authors' own field monitoring with Sentek capacitance probes across commercial potato fields in 2018 and 2019 and their own ET estimates by three methods.
rows.notes: All fields were scheduled with soil moisture probes (35% TAW depletion trigger); there was no non-sensor control, so no water saving attributable to the sensors is measured. The paper reports only the applied irrigation amount (777 <U+00B1> 36 mm) and ET estimates; the abstract's statement that probe-based scheduling 'improved irrigation water management' is an assertion not backed by a comparative result. No 15% water reduction or farmer survey on time/effort is reported. The study supports only a precondition (sensors characterise root-zone soil water and the 40 cm effective rooting depth useful for scheduling), so upstream is set to true.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a descriptive monitoring/ET-comparison study on sprinkler-irrigated potato with no treatment comparison involving sensor versus non-sensor scheduling and no yield measurements; the specific figures in the review passage (6.6% yield increase, 15% water reduction, farmer-reported time savings) are not from this paper and seem to be misattributed.
